name: PT Satria Antaran Prima Tbk

frontmatter.title: SAPX Express: a leveraged sub-scale courier priced for a recovery its cash flow does not yet fund
frontmatter.summary: We stay SELL. The nine months to September 2026 produced the first positive operating cash flow in the record and receivables have started to release, so the bear case is less mechanical than it was. The price still capitalises a recovery the courier economics do not support: revenue is shrinking, working capital absorbs much of every sale, interest consumes most of operating profit, and the operating business is worth well below the enterprise value the market pays.
thesis: Revenue is still shrinking: FY2025 fell a quarter on FY2024 and the nine months to September 2026 were down again, on lost courier and cash-on-delivery volume rather than price [S6][S3].
The margin is at the nine-month actual, not improving: the FY2026E EBITDA uplift over FY2025 comes from depreciation falling as leases and the fleet run off, not from operating leverage [S4][S3].

Cash conversion has turned: 9M2026 operating cash flow was positive and receivables fell, which removes the mechanical core of the old bear case but does not fund the debt maturing inside a year [S3].

Leverage still owns the equity: bank debt due within twelve months is 98.3 IDR bnbn, of which 93.0 IDR bnbn is short-term, secured on 64.9 IDR bnbn of the company's own deposits, and interest absorbs most of operating profit [S3].

The balance sheet holds 64.9 IDR bnbn of pledged cash, a 45.3 IDR bnbn Level three stake and a 20.7 IDR bnbn land down payment; we credit all three after probability haircuts and the target is still Rp152 [S3].
The price implies 14.5x EV/EBITDA on our FY2026E against a 7.2x peer median, and 1.0x book for a business earning a low single-digit return on equity [S0].

blocks.text: We maintain coverage of PT Satria Antaran Prima Tbk (SAPX Express) with a **SELL** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp152**, -40.3% from the Rp254 price at the data-pack date and with no dividend expected (Rp0). The stock is not expensive because the courier business is bad at the margin — it is expensive because the market is paying for a franchise whose revenue is still shrinking, whose balance sheet is funded by bank debt that matures inside a year, and whose free float is 8.9%.

This revision changes six things after the red team's first pass. We restated working capital from the filings: the data pack's series included restricted cash, which is pledged collateral and belongs in the bridge, not in operating working capital, and that error had inflated both the historical cash burn and the forecast release. We took the nine-month 2026 cash-flow actual seriously: operating cash flow was 8.1 IDR bnbn against a large outflow a year earlier, and receivables fell [S3]. We aligned the EV/EBITDA cross-check to the restated EBITDA instead of the pack's, dropped the P/E cross-check rather than keep a trough-earnings capitalisation at weight, and probability-weighted the two non-certain bridge items. We also corrected the governance section: a rights-issue mandate does exist in the record, unimplemented. The result is a higher target than the first draft but the same rating.

The variant view is simple and uncomfortable. The company's profit improvement is real but comes from the cost line, not the revenue line: revenue fell a quarter in FY2025 and by double digits again in the nine months to September 2026, while operating expenses fell by more than a third [S6][S3]. What is left is a business that earns 3.6% at the operating line, pays IDR13.3bn of interest against IDR16.2bn of operating profit, and has only just begun to convert profit into cash [S3]. Management stabilised the margin; it has not shown it can stabilise the top line.

Three things move the value. First, revenue: operating working capital runs at 40.0% of sales on the nine-month balance sheet, so growth is a cash consumer rather than a value driver, and the DCF's operating value is lower than a peer multiple implies. Second, the discount rate: a levered microcap with a 0.8x debt-to-equity ratio carries a cost of equity of 13.0%, at the top of the compounder card's IDR band, and a WACC of 10.5%. Third, the balance sheet: we credit the 64.9 IDR bnbn of pledged deposits, the 45.3 IDR bnbn Mitra Samudra stake after a minority and marketability haircut and the 20.7 IDR bnbn land down payment at half weight, and the DCF still lands at Rp79.

What the market is paying, on our numbers, is 14.5x EV/EBITDA for FY2026E, 87.4x the earnings we forecast for FY2027E, and 1.0x book. The EV/EBITDA comparison is the cleanest statement of the premium: against the 7.2x peer median the market pays up for a declining, thinly traded, family- and GDEX-controlled name [S6]. Our target sits -40.3% from the price; the bear case is Rp83, the base case Rp123 and the bull case Rp278.

SAPX Express is a Jakarta-based express courier: it picks up, consolidates, line-hauls and delivers parcels and documents across Indonesia, and sells adjacent services — cash on delivery, warehousing and fulfilment, mailroom outsourcing, packaging and international shipping [S0]. The company was founded in 2014, listed in 2018 and has never established a subsidiary, so the consolidated accounts are the operating company itself [S6]. It employed 5,197 person people at the end of FY2025 [S6]; the data pack's headcount of 135.0 is wrong and we do not use it.

The network is a hybrid of owned hubs and third-party reach. The company discloses that it covers the great majority of Indonesian districts for regular delivery and a slightly smaller set for cash-on-delivery and non-COD services, operating through distribution centres, a very large network of agent drop points, retail outlets and a fleet of blind vans [S6]. The economics are visible in the cost line: the largest single direct cost is freight and courier payments to third parties, which is what an asset-light, agent-based last-mile model looks like [S4]. Rent and short-term leases are the second structural cost, and the company capitalises a right-of-use asset for its premises [S4].

Revenue is overwhelmingly Greater Jakarta. Of IDR523.1bn of FY2025 revenue, 426 IDR bnbn came from Jabodetabek and the balance from outside it [S4]. There is no volume or price disclosure in the financial statements, and no customer-concentration table, which is itself a limitation on how much of the revenue build we can decompose: management says only that the FY2025 decline came from courier revenue and cash-on-delivery revenue [S6].

Strategy since the pandemic has been a retreat from volume to margin. Management describes a selective investment approach, with spending aimed at network strengthening, digital technology and service quality, and states plainly that competition has intensified and that the operating environment in FY2025 was difficult [S6]. The observable result is a smaller company with a better margin: gross margin of 18.4% in FY2025 on a much smaller revenue base, against 24.4% in FY2023 when revenue was larger [S4].

Ownership is concentrated and strategic. PT Satria Investama Perdana holds 46.6% of the shares; the Malaysian GDEX group — Gdex Sea, Gd Express Carrier and Gd Valueguard — holds the rest of the controlling block, and the public holds the residual [S6]. GDEX is a regional express operator, so SAPX sits inside a cross-border logistics group rather than being an orphan listing, but the relationship has not produced visible revenue synergies in the reported numbers: outside-Jakarta revenue is a small fraction of the total and fell in FY2025 [S4].

Position in the value chain is weak. SAPX is a challenger in a market where the largest parcel flows are controlled by the e-commerce platforms and by national networks with far greater density. It buys line-haul and last-mile capacity from third parties, which caps gross margin, and it sells to corporate shippers and online sellers who can switch networks on price. That combination — no pricing power, no scale advantage, no switching costs — is why we treat the business as a low-return utility rather than a compounder, and why the compounder card's reinvestment test, set out in the valuation section, fails [S4][S6].

Indonesian express delivery grew out of the e-commerce boom and is now a mature, brutal price market. The structural feature that matters for SAPX is that the largest parcel generators own or favour their own delivery networks, so independent couriers compete for the residual volume of smaller platforms and social-commerce sellers — a segment where price is the only real differentiator. The company itself frames FY2025 as a year of weak consumer confidence, fiscal and monetary adjustment, changing demand patterns and intensifying competition, and attributes the revenue fall to courier and cash-on-delivery volume [S6]. That is the management's own account of a market in which it lost share.

Express delivery in Indonesia has three tiers: platform-owned networks that carry their own marketplace parcels, national independents with dense own-hub coverage, and regional or niche operators that buy capacity. Fixed costs are hubs, sortation and line-haul; variable costs are courier payments, fuel and packaging. Because the platforms set the clearing price for standard parcels, independent operators earn margin only on corporate accounts, documents, cash-on-delivery handling and value-added services. Consolidation among the independents has been the norm, and sub-scale operators either specialise or shrink.

Competitive analysis, five forces. **Rivalry** is high and worsening: the company names intensifying industry competition as a principal challenge in both the FY2025 management report and the outlook for 2026 [S6]. **Buyer power** is high: corporate shippers and online sellers tender volume on price, and the company discloses no long-term customer contracts. **Supplier power** is moderate: line-haul and courier partners are numerous, but the company depends on them for reach and pays them the largest single cost line [S4]. **Threat of entry** is high at the low end, because an agent-based network can be assembled quickly, although the platforms' own networks now occupy the volume. **Substitutes** are the platforms' captive delivery arms and, at the margin, consolidated logistics providers that bundle warehousing with delivery.

Regulation is light-touch at the operating level — postal and courier licensing, customs for cross-border, and the standard IDX disclosure regime. The material regulatory exposure is financial rather than operational: the company's bank facilities are short-term and secured, and 64.9 IDR bnbn of its own cash is pledged as collateral against them [S3]. There is no tariff or licence regime that protects the incumbent, and no subsidy that supports the challenger.

We cannot size SAPX's market share from any primary source: the annual report contains no market-share estimate, and we have not substituted a third-party figure. What can be said with evidence is directional. Revenue fell from IDR682.5bn in FY2024 to IDR523.1bn in FY2025 and to 346 IDR bnbn in the nine months to September 2026 [S4][S3], while management describes a growing market driven by digital trade [S6]. Falling revenue in a growing market is share loss, whatever the absolute number.

Moat assessment: none that we can evidence. There are no network effects in a business that rents its reach, no switching costs disclosed, no brand pricing power visible in a 18.4% gross margin that has fallen from 24.4%, and no cost advantage against national networks with more parcels per route [S4]. The GDEX shareholding is a potential distribution advantage across borders, but the reported numbers do not yet show it: outside-Jakarta revenue declined in FY2025 [S4]. Under the house growth identity, growth equals reinvestment multiplied by incremental return on invested capital; with incremental returns below the cost of capital, more growth would destroy value, which is precisely what our DCF shows.

External influences are three. The rupiah and the BI rate set the cost of the company's debt when it rolls: the Permata facilities are fixed-rate today at 8.2% and the LK states there are no floating-rate interest-bearing liabilities, but they mature in June 2027 and reprice at whatever the market then offers [S3]. Interest expense has more than quadrupled across the record as debt was rolled and grown [S4]. Fuel and transport costs pass through the direct cost line with a lag. And the e-commerce cycle decides whether there is volume to bid for at all — a macro variable the company does not control and cannot hedge.

**The revenue line.** Revenue peaked at IDR682.5bn in FY2024 and fell to IDR523.1bn in FY2025, a decline management attributes to courier and cash-on-delivery revenue [S6]. The nine months to September 2026 were 346 IDR bnbn, running at the -13.9% full-year decline we forecast on the same trend [S3]. We hold the fourth quarter at that nine-month run-rate rather than assume a stabilisation nobody has sourced: FY2026E revenue is IDR450.4bn (-13.9%), then 2.0% and 3.0% as the lost volume annualises against a smaller base. We assume no recapture of the FY2024 book: there is no disclosed contract, capacity expansion or client win that would justify it. The Q4 2025 base was already weak, so this is the least heroic of the available revenue paths, not a punitive one.

**Margins and the D&A restatement.** The data pack's depreciation is a fragment. The FY2025 financial statements charge 14.8 IDR bnbn of depreciation — fixed-asset depreciation plus right-of-use depreciation — against the pack's reported figure, because the Indonesian cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and the pack picks up only the G&A line [S4]. FY2024 is 16.3 IDR bnbn on the same basis. We restate both years, which lifts historical EBITDA to IDR25.0bn (4.8% margin) and changes every multiple that uses it. This remains the single most important data correction in the model.

On the restated basis the operating story is the nine-month actual, not a forecast improvement. Gross margin was 18.4% in FY2025 and 19.0% in our forecast, exactly the nine-month 2026 actual; operating expenses ran at 15.4% of revenue in the nine months, and we hold them there rather than assume further cuts [S3]. That gives an operating margin of 3.6% and EBITDA of IDR24.5bn — lower than FY2025's IDR25.0bn because revenue falls faster than the cost base, even though depreciation decays as the fleet and leased premises run off (1.8% of revenue in FY2026E against IDR14.8bn of depreciation in FY2025), not because the business is expanding. The arithmetic is in facts F1, F2 and F17.

**Below the operating line.** Interest expense was IDR12.6bn in FY2025, above operating profit of IDR10.1bn [S4]; in the nine months to September 2026 the filing shows 9.6 IDR bnbn, against IDR13.3bn in our full-year forecast (we hold the contracted rate on the year-end debt rather than annualise nine months of a shrinking balance), against debt that rose from IDR161.9bn to 98.3 IDR bnbn of bank debt maturing inside twelve months and 93.0 IDR bnbn of short-term bank loans at the third quarter [S3]. We use the contracted 8.2% rate disclosed on the Permata facilities, not a market guess. Net profit is therefore a residual of financing, not of operations: IDR0.7bn in FY2025 and IDR2.2bn in our forecast, on an effective tax rate of 22.0%. Return on equity is 0.4% for FY2025 and 1.1% by FY2027E — better, still far below the cost of equity.

**Cash flow and working capital.** This section is rewritten on the latest filing, because the first draft was stale. Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025 (-6.7 IDR bnbn) and FY2024 (-27.8 IDR bnbn) [S4], but the nine months to September 2026 produced 8.1 IDR bnbn of operating cash inflow against a large outflow in the prior-year period, on cash receipts from customers of 353 IDR bnbn against revenue of 346 IDR bnbn, with trade receivables down to 175 IDR bnbn from 178 IDR bnbn gross at the prior year-end [S3]. That is a change in cash conversion, not a reclassification: the receivables book is being collected, and the company's own cash-flow statement shows it. FY2026E operating cash flow is positive in our model and FCFF is IDR9.0bn; the rating does not change on it because the cash is going to interest and to debt maturing inside a year, not to equity.

The working-capital history is also restated [S4][S3]. The data pack's operating working capital included current restricted cash — the pledged collateral — which is separately credited in the valuation bridge; on the operating definition, working capital was IDR151.8bn at end-2024 and IDR174.6bn at end-2025 (facts F29-F30), and the FY2024 FCFF that the pack reported as deeply negative is IDR-18.3bn on our restatement, against filed operating cash flow of -27.8 IDR bnbn and FY2024 capex of 4.1 IDR bnbn. That reconciliation does not tie arithmetically and we say so rather than dress it: taking after-tax interest back and capex off the filed operating cash flow still leaves our restated FY2024A FCFF short of the filed figure, and the gap is the FY2023 opening working capital, which the data pack measured inclusive of restricted cash and which we cannot re-derive from the archived filings — the FY2025 LK carries only the 2024 comparative. FY2024A FCFF is therefore not like-for-like with the filed cash-flow statement, and the gap does not reach the forecast years because their delta-NWC is built on one basis from FY2024 onwards and the marginal ratio is set on the 2026 actual. The nine-month 2026 balance sheet gives an operating working-capital ratio of 40.0% of annualised revenue (fact F31), which is what we hold: the FY2026E revenue decline therefore releases little, and every point of growth afterwards is charged the same ratio. We could not re-derive FY2022 and FY2023 from the archived filings — the FY2025 LK carries only the 2024 comparative — so those two pack years remain the residual limitation in the reconciliation, and they do not affect the forecast because the marginal ratio is set on the 2026 actual.

Capex has run far below depreciation: IDR2.2bn in FY2025 against 14.8 IDR bnbn of depreciation [S4]. The asset base is shrinking — net property, plant and equipment at the third quarter, including right-of-use assets, was 16.3 IDR bnbn, of which the owned fixed assets are almost fully depreciated and the rest is leased premises [S3] — and the company has instead advanced 20.7 IDR bnbn for land in Depok, West Java, where permitting is still in progress [S4]. We quote the filing figure wherever the asset base is described; the model's fixed-asset line is carried on the pack's presentation, which does not separate right-of-use assets, and that presentation is the residual reconciliation limitation on this line. We forecast capex at 1.4% of revenue, enough to replace depreciation in steady state; we do not extend the current under-investment into perpetuity, and we do not credit the land with more than half its book cost in the bridge.

**Balance sheet and debt.** At the third quarter of 2026 the company had 98.3 IDR bnbn of bank debt maturing inside twelve months, of which 93.0 IDR bnbn is short-term bank loans secured on 64.9 IDR bnbn of its own restricted deposits, plus lease liabilities and IDR20.2bn of unrestricted cash at the FY2025 year-end [S3]. The long-term bank debt is small and amortising; the refinancing risk sits in the revolving lines, which the LK shows extended to 25 June 2027 and repricing at that point [S3]. Net debt to EBITDA on our restated numbers is 5.9x — serviceable only if the revenue base holds and the banks keep rolling short lines. Equity is IDR212.1bn, of which a large part is the revaluation surplus on the Mitra Samudra stake carried through other comprehensive income [S4].

**Earnings quality.** Running the house screens on the latest actual: the accruals ratio was adverse in FY2024-FY2025, but 9M2026 operating cash flow of 8.1 IDR bnbn against net profit of IDR2.2bn for the full-year forecast reverses the sign, so the "earnings ahead of cash" conclusion is no longer current and we withdraw it. One divergence flag still fires: receivables are large relative to revenue and the allowance is only around a fiftieth of the 178 IDR bnbn gross book — thin for a ledger that has been slow, with 8.9 IDR bnbn more than ninety days overdue [S3]. On the IDX regime screens we found no special notation or administrative sanction in FY2025 [S6], but the status that now applies is the high-shareholding-concentration list: SAPX is among the HSC names the exchange removed from the IHSG calculation with effect from 13 November 2026, the data-pack price date [S9][S10], on a free float of 8.9% [S0]. We also found no auditor downgrade (the FY2025 opinion is unqualified from the Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang dan Rekan firm), and small related-party balances — a modest payable to a related party and a legacy related-party loan repaid in FY2024 [S4]. Structure flags: a free float of 8.9%, no dividend history, an unimplemented rights-issue mandate (section six), and a controlling family stake alongside a strategic Malaysian holder [S6]. We classify the receivables issue as optics-class rather than manipulation-class: it is disclosed, aged and provided for, but it justifies a discount, not a pass.

This is a compounder-card name in a sector where the card's test decides the method. The growth identity — growth equals reinvestment rate multiplied by return on incremental invested capital — fails: incremental capital here goes into receivables at 40.0% of sales, and the return on that capital is the operating margin the company actually earns, which is below its cost of capital. When a business earns less than its cost of capital, growth destroys value, and the right method is a cash-flow model that lets that happen rather than a multiple that capitalises a growth story. We therefore weight DCF at 70.0% and keep EV/EBITDA as the single cross-check at 30.0%. We treat the peer multiples with suspicion because the peer set is a mixed bag of shipping, aviation services and taxi operators [S0], but a market-based cross-check is still the honest discipline on a house DCF. We dropped the P/E cross-check rather than keep it at weight, for the reason set out below.

The discount rate is built by the engine from the house macro deck: risk-free at 7.4% (the deck's rupiah risk-free with the Indonesia default spread of 1.6% netted out), mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, unlevered beta 0.9x for the sector, relevered to 1.5x at a 0.8x debt-to-equity ratio, giving a cost of equity of 13.0% and a WACC of 10.5% at a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt, a 22.0% tax rate and equity/debt weights of 56.0%/44.0%. Two points of house discipline apply. The mechanical build lands at a cost of equity above the compounder card's IDR band; we could not source a size or liquidity premium large enough to defend the excess, so the base case holds the top of the band (13.0% after a -2.5% band adjustment) and the bear case adds a point. On debt, the P&L uses the contracted 8.2% rate disclosed on the Permata facilities, while the WACC uses the deck's marginal corporate rate of 9.4% because those facilities must be refinanced inside a year; using the contracted rate in the WACC as well would cut the WACC by about half a point and raise the DCF by roughly a twentieth, so the present setup biases value down, not up. Explicit liquidity discount is 0.0%, discussed in section five.

The primary method produces an enterprise value of IDR97.6bnbn for the operating business and equity of Rp79 a share. Terminal value is 49.7% of the total, which is the honest consequence of a business with no moat: we fade revenue growth to 4.0% in the terminal period, below the deck's implied nominal GDP path (real GDP 529.0% plus CPI 328.0%), and because return on capital sits below the cost of capital that terminal growth is not a value driver. The gap to nominal GDP is deliberate rather than cautious: a sub-scale courier in the deck's CAUTIOUS, balance-of-payments-pressure regime should not be capitalised at the economy's nominal growth when its own incremental returns are below the cost of capital. The multiple-survival test confirms the point: the DCF's implied exit value is below what the market pays today, so buying the shares is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume — it is paying today for a re-rating that our model does not support.

The cross-checks diverge, and we explain rather than smooth. The EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp177 (7.2x peer median) is 122.4% above the DCF. The basis is now consistent with the restated history: the peer median is a trailing EV/EBITDA multiple taken from the pack's logistics and transport peer set [S0], applied to restated LTM EBITDA of IDR25.0bn rather than to the pack's under-depreciated figure. The divergence is the method, not a data error: the cash-flow model charges the company for its working-capital intensity and fades growth, while the peer multiple capitalises today's EBITDA as if neither applied. We keep the multiple at weight because it is the market-based cross-check, but the DCF is the view and the multiple is the ceiling a strategic buyer might pay. We dropped the P/E cross-check rather than keep it at weight: the engine applies a peer trailing multiple to last restated LTM net profit, which is trough FY2025 earnings of IDR0.7bn, and a trough-earnings capitalisation is not a value estimate. The forward P/E of 87.4x on our FY2027E is a monitoring multiple, not an input.

The bridge is where we refuse to be lazy, and this revision stops pretending its items are certain. The data pack counts only unrestricted cash, so we add back: 64.9 IDR bnbn of restricted cash pledged against the bank loans (an asset the company owns, offset against debt it owes) at full weight [S3]; 45.3 IDR bnbn for the minority stake in PT Mitra Samudra Indonesia, carried at an appraised Level three fair value several times cost and unchanged through three reporting dates, at a probability weight because a minority stake in an unlisted company is not realisable at the appraisal [S3]; 7.4 IDR bnbn of estimated income-tax refund for FY2025, still outstanding at 30 September 2026, at a probability weight below one [S3]; and 20.7 IDR bnbn of land down payment in Depok, still in permitting, at half weight [S4]. The old draft claimed the bridge total was close to the balance sheet's "other assets less other liabilities" plug. That cross-check was wrong, because other assets are not the same population and the plug carries lease and tax balances; we withdraw it. The bridge note on the tax item is the correction of this round: the claim outstanding at 30 September 2026 is the FY2025 one of 7.4 IDR bnbn; what the company collected during 2026 was the prior-year claim that stood at the 2025 year-end, so the remaining claim is cash we expect later, not cash already inside net debt, and we weight it below one for the audit lag [S3]. The probability-weighted bridge is disclosed in the model and the target above is struck after it. We do not add the deferred tax asset or the security deposits, and we do not net out the employee-benefit liability.

The three inputs that carry most of the value are the gross margin, the revenue growth path and the working-capital ratio. The grid shows the uncomfortable result of the working-capital assumption: because growth absorbs cash at 40.0% of sales and the return on that cash is below the cost of capital, more growth lowers the DCF value. The value is highest where margin is better and revenue is smaller — which is exactly the corner the market's price requires. A two-point move in gross margin is worth more than a two-point move in growth, which is why we treat the margin line as the only genuine upside lever.

What today's price implies. At Rp254 the market pays 1.0x our FY2026E book value, 14.5x our FY2026E EBITDA and 87.4x our FY2027E earnings. LTM EBITDA is IDR25.0bn and FY2026E EBITDA is IDR24.5bn, so the price is not being set on a stale trough figure. After crediting the probability-weighted bridge, the price still values the operating business at a premium to the 7.2x peer median — a smaller premium than the headline EV/EBITDA comparison implies, but a premium nonetheless. Our reverse DCF cannot bracket the price with any revenue-growth path because the required combination is higher margin *and* lower revenue: the sensitivity grid reaches the traded price only in its best-margin, worst-growth corner. That is not a growth path; it is a margin-and-shrink story, and it is the honest version of the extreme-call argument the first draft made too strongly. The bull case, which adds a GDEX transaction to the operating improvement, does reach the price; the base and bear cases do not.

**Downside risks, likelihood times impact.** *Refinancing (medium likelihood, high impact):* 98.3 IDR bnbn of bank debt matures inside twelve months, of which 93.0 IDR bnbn is short-term and secured on 64.9 IDR bnbn of the company's own deposits; no committed long-dated facility is disclosed, so a bank declining to roll forces asset sales or a capital raise [S3]. *Receivables (medium, high):* 178 IDR bnbn gross, 8.9 IDR bnbn more than ninety days overdue and an allowance of around a fiftieth of the book; a single large account failing would hit equity [S3]. *Revenue erosion (high, high):* the company has lost volume in two consecutive periods and has no disclosed contract book; another platform shift could take the base lower again [S6]. *Margin (medium, medium):* gross margin is at the nine-month actual and the cost cuts have already been taken; a further volume decline spreads fixed sortation and courier-partner costs over fewer parcels [S3][S4]. *Interest rates (low, medium):* the facilities are fixed-rate today at 8.2%, but they reprice at the June 2027 maturity; each point of repricing is material against IDR16.2bn of operating profit [S3]. *Commodity and fuel (medium, low):* transport and fuel are direct costs with a lag in pass-through. *Currency (low, low):* revenue is domestic and debt is rupiah, so direct FX exposure is small; the deck's rupiah path matters only through imported equipment. *Governance and liquidity (medium, high):* a 8.9% float, an HSC listing that took the shares out of the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026 [S9][S10], and a history of exchange scrutiny mean the price can move on very little flow [S7].

On governance specifically: the exchange flagged the shares for unusual market activity at the end of 2023 after a sharp run-up, and the company subsequently denied internet rumours of a strategic tie-up with a global courier, confirming that it had no merger, acquisition or partnership plan [S7][S8]. Neither is evidence of wrongdoing; both are evidence that the price is not informationally efficient, which cuts against relying on the market's mark as a valuation anchor.

**Liquidity, reconciled.** The first draft argued both ways, and the red team was right to say so. Three-month value traded is above the fund's floor, which is why the engine applies a 0.0% explicit discount: the house rule keys the discount to value traded, and above the top tier it is zero. That does not make the stock liquid in any economic sense. A 8.9% float on IDR211,666,658,200.0bn of market capitalisation is a small absolute pool, and daily turnover of that size implies the free float changing hands repeatedly rather than a deep market. Both statements can hold, and we now say so plainly: the valuation discount is zero under the house rule, the position-size cap is the binding constraint, and the price can gap on modest flow. The "shares almost never trade" claim in the first draft is withdrawn.

On the **controlling blocks**, which the first draft did not price and the last round mislabelled: PT Satria Investama Perdana, the controlling family, holds 46.6% [S6], and the GDEX group — Gdex Sea, Gd Express Carrier and Gd Valueguard — holds the balance of the controlling block alongside it [S6]. The public float is 8.9% and the register has not changed through FY2025 [S6]. That structure is an option on a strategic take-out, a group capital injection or a cross-border volume transfer, and it is why a quarter of the probability mass sits in the bull case rather than the near-zero a pure operating view would justify. We put no separate option value in the bridge — there is no disclosed price, mandate or transaction — but the bull case is explicit: a take-out by the two controlling parties together at the peer EV/EBITDA, plus the operating improvement, reaches Rp278, which is above the Rp254 traded price. Either block alone can block a transaction and neither has disclosed one, which is why the take-out needs both and why it sits in the tail rather than the base case. The first draft's claim that even the bull case could not reach the price is withdrawn; it was an artefact of the un-restated EBITDA basis.

The **asset backing** is real but softer than it looks. Book equity is IDR212.1bn, or Rp255 a share, roughly the market capitalisation, and there is no goodwill on the balance sheet [S4]. But the assets are mostly receivables and marks, not plant: gross property, plant and equipment is 96.0 IDR bnbn against accumulated depreciation of 90.8 IDR bnbn, so the fixed-asset base is almost fully depreciated, and the largest single non-operating asset is the Level three Mitra Samudra stake [S4][S3]. A book-value floor exists, but it is a liquidation floor, not an earnings floor, and we do not use it as a valuation method.

The scenarios shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts, so the two risks we rank highest are inside the numbers rather than only in the prose. **Bear (25.0%, Rp83):** volume keeps eroding, revenue growth four points a year below base and gross margin two points lower as fixed sortation and courier-partner costs spread over fewer parcels; working capital worsens by ten points of revenue as slow receivables are not collected and one large account is written down; and the discount rate rises a point because a revolving facility is not rolled. **Base (50.0%, Rp123):** the nine-month revenue decline annualises, growth returns at two to four points nominal, margin holds at the nine-month level, working capital stays at 40.0% of sales. **Bull (25.0%, Rp278):** the GDEX cross-border relationship and corporate accounts add volume at the current margin, gross margin gains two points on mix, receivables are collected faster and a transaction agreed by both controlling blocks — the family and GDEX together — removes the refinancing overhang, cutting the discount rate a point.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a full year of positive operating cash flow with receivables still falling — the nine-month actual is most of the way there, and confirmation would lift the bear case; a term-out of the revolving lines into a committed long-dated facility; a signed volume contract with a platform or a large corporate shipper, disclosed in a filing; two consecutive quarters of revenue growth with stable gross margin; or a sale of the Mitra Samudra stake at or above its carrying value. Any two of these would move us toward HOLD; none alone is enough while the price sits this far above the base case.

**Ownership and control.** PT Satria Investama Perdana holds 46.6% of the shares and is the controlling shareholder; the GDEX group holds the rest of the controlling block, and the public holds 8.9% [S6]. The insider share is 91.1%. There is no institutional ownership in the data pack. A float this thin on a company of this size is the single most important governance fact about the equity: the price is set at the margin by a very small number of shares, and the company's own disclosure confirms the shareholder register did not change through FY2025 [S6]. The exchange now treats the name accordingly: SAPX sits on the high-shareholding-concentration list, whose category the exchange defines by near-total concentration of the register in ten holders [S10], and the shares were removed from the IHSG calculation from 13 November 2026 [S9][S10]. The consequence for us is not a mechanical index sale — the name was never an index weight of consequence — but three things we carry: the liquidity argument in section five is reinforced rather than weakened; no discount-rate change is made for it, because the WACC already prices a levered microcap at the top of the house band; and the exchange's minimum free-float requirement, with compliance due by 31 March 2029, is a live obligation on a 8.9% float, so a sell-down or a rights issue by the controlling blocks is a dated event we monitor rather than a hypothetical [S0][S9][S10].

**Related parties and structure.** The company has never established a subsidiary, holds no bonds or other listed securities, and its related-party balances are small — a modest payable to a related party and a related-party loan repaid in FY2024 [S4][S6]. The one structural item worth monitoring is the minority stake in PT Mitra Samudra Indonesia, an unlisted technology company, carried at an appraised fair value that is several times its cost and marked through other comprehensive income [S3]. That valuation is Level three, appraised by an independent firm, and it accounts for a meaningful share of book equity; a write-down would be an accounting event, not a cash one, but it would remove support from the book value multiple.

**Pledges and corporate actions.** No pledge of the controlling shareholders' shares is disclosed; the pledges in the accounts are the company's own restricted deposits securing its bank facilities [S3]. We correct the first draft here: a rights-issue mandate does exist in the record. The EGMS of 21 August 2023 approved a Capital Increase with Pre-emptive Rights (PM-HMETD I); the FY2025 annual report records that the board explained its non-implementation and the AGMS accepted that explanation [S6]. No issue size, price or use of proceeds is disclosed, and no new mandate has been granted, so we do not model an issuance — but for a company with 98.3 IDR bnbn of debt maturing inside a year, an unimplemented rights mandate is a live financing option and a per-share dilution risk, and it is a signpost we watch at the 2027 AGM. We found no dividend declared or paid in any year, and the FY2025 cash-flow statement shows no dividend payment [S4].

**Board, auditor and enforcement.** The FY2025 accounts were audited by the Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang dan Rekan firm with an unqualified opinion, and the company states it received no administrative sanction in FY2025 [S6][S4]. The board and management were reshuffled in 2025 with a new finance director; the president director has been in place through the period covered by the filings [S6]. The exchange's unusual-market-activity notice at the end of 2023 and the company's subsequent clarification are the only regulatory events we found, and we note them as market-integrity context rather than as findings [S7][S8].

**ESG exposures.** The material social issue in this business is labour in the courier and agent network: a large share of last-mile delivery is performed by third-party couriers and agents, whose terms the company does not disclose in the annual report. Environmental exposure is modest in absolute terms — a fleet of vans and leased premises — but the company's sustainability reporting is thin on measurable targets, and we would not pay for an ESG premium here. Governance is where the discount belongs: a thin float, a concentrated register and a history of price volatility that attracted exchange scrutiny [S4][S6][S7][S8].

The near-term calendar is mostly financial, not operational. The FY2026 audited accounts, due within four months of the year-end, are the first full-year test of whether the cost-led margin repair survives on a smaller revenue base and whether the nine-month cash conversion holds for a full year; we will compare revenue, gross margin, operating cash flow and receivables against the forecasts in section three [S4][S6]. The June 2027 maturity of the Permata revolving facilities is the single largest event: the terms on which those lines are rolled or replaced decide whether the equity is a going concern or an option on the assets. The annual general meeting follows, and with no dividend history the interesting question is whether the board seeks a new capital-raising mandate, not what it distributes. The Depok land permitting outcome matters because the land down payment is carried in our valuation bridge at half weight; a failed permit would impair it, and a completed sortation hub would be the first capacity addition in years.

Between updates we monitor four numbers: the quarterly revenue trend, because it decides whether the base has stabilised; gross margin, because it is the only lever management has shown it can pull; trade receivables, their ageing and the allowance against them, because they are the cash sink even after the third-quarter release; and the short-term bank lines and their collateral, because they are the refinancing risk. We also watch the register: any change in either controlling block or the free float would change the liquidity picture and the price-setting mechanism, and any move on the 2023 rights mandate would change the share count [S3][S4][S6].

Indonesian courier equities have historically traded on growth expectations rather than on cash flow, and the sector's smaller names have spent the past several years de-rating as platform-owned networks took the volume. The pattern is familiar from other consumer and logistics franchises in the region: a premium multiple attached to a story, followed by a long de-rating once the growth stops. Our method card treats that de-rating base rate as the default for quality stories, and it applies with more force to a leveraged sub-scale operator than to a market leader.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the fourth quarter at the nine-month run-rate: 9M2026 revenue of Rp346.46bn was 13.9% below 9M2025, and applying that same year-on-year decline to Q4 2025 (Rp120.8bn) gives FY2026E revenue of Rp450.5bn, a 13.9% decline on FY2025. No Q4 stabilisation is sourced, so none is assumed; FY2027E+ returns to 2-4% nominal growth as the 2025 volume purge (courier and COD revenue, per the FY2025 MD&A) annualises against a smaller base. No recapture of the 2024 book is assumed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 19.0%, the 9M2026 actual (gross profit Rp65.8bn on revenue Rp346.5bn), held flat. FY2025 was 18.4% and FY2024 20.7%; the 2025 direct-cost reset held the margin at the smaller revenue base and the nine-month 2026 figure is the last actual. No further price-led recovery is assumed because courier pricing remains competitive.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 15.4%: 9M2026 actual 15.35% (Rp53.2bn on Rp346.5bn) after the 35.5% operating-expense cut the company reports for FY2025 (16.5% of revenue). Held flat from here - no further efficiency is claimed, and no rebound in spending is assumed either.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 1.83% in FY2026E: 9M2026 depreciation Rp6.187bn annualised to Rp8.25bn on revenue of Rp450.5bn (the same absolute charge, lower revenue base). Total depreciation was Rp14.85bn in FY2025 against a net fixed-asset plus right-of-use book of Rp21.6bn at end-2025, so the charge decays as the fleet and leased premises run off: 1.60% in FY2027E falling to 1.45% by FY2029E.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: 1.4% (about Rp6.6bn a year) - the level at which capex replaces depreciation plus the Depok land and sortation works. FY2025 capex was Rp2.21bn against Rp14.85bn of depreciation, so the asset base is currently shrinking; we do not extend that under-investment forever.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 40% of revenue, the 9M2026 actual on the operating definition: operating working capital of Rp180.8bn at 30 September 2026 (receivables, other receivables, inventories, prepaid expenses, prepaid taxes and advances less trade and other payables, accruals, taxes payable and customer advances; cash and restricted cash excluded) over annualised 9M2026 revenue of Rp462.0bn = 39.1%. The ratio rose from 33.4% at end-2025 and 22.2% at end-2024 as revenue fell faster than receivables; held at 40% because no collection improvement beyond the Q3 release is evidenced. The data pack's history is restated in facts F29-F31 to the same operating definition.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22% statutory. 9M2026 tax charge Rp1.30bn on pre-tax Rp5.92bn = 22.0%; FY2025 was distorted by a loss-making tax computation and Rp7.4bn of prepaid article-23 tax.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8.2%: the LK discloses contracted effective rates of 8.30% and 8.15% on the two Permata revolving facilities (simple average 8.225%) and states there are no floating-rate borrowings, so the rate is fixed. The P&L cross-check agrees: FY2025 interest Rp12.61bn on Rp148.2bn of bank debt plus leases and 9M2026 Rp9.57bn annualised on Rp166bn both land near 8%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.5% on the cash the model carries. The LK's interest income (Rp1.9bn annualised) is mostly earned on the Rp64.9bn of restricted deposits, which the valuation carries as a bridge item rather than as cash.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero - debt held flat at the 30 September 2026 level. The company has rolled short-term bank lines rather than repaid them, and we give no credit for deleveraging that is not in evidence.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: -Rp1.0bn a year: bank administration charges of Rp1.2bn against other income, excluding the Rp1.7-2.1bn gains on vehicle disposal that flattered 2025 and 9M2026. No disposal gains are credited in the forecast.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 0% - the company has never established a subsidiary (AR 2025).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 0% - no dividend has been declared or paid in any year of the record, and the FY2025 cash-flow statement shows no dividend payment. Interest and working capital absorb the cash.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 0% - 833.33m shares issued and fully paid, unchanged through FY2025 and 9M2026. A rights issue mandate exists in the record but not in force: the EGMS of 21 August 2023 approved PM-HMETD I, the board reported it was not implemented in the FY2025 annual report, and the AGMS accepted that explanation (AR 2025 p.45 and p.127). No size, price or use of proceeds is disclosed and no new mandate has been granted, so no issuance is modelled; a discounted rights issue remains a live structural risk, flagged in section 6.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%, below the house macro deck's implied long-run nominal GDP of about 8.6% (real GDP 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%), and the rate the explicit forecast fades to in 2031-35. The gap is deliberate: a sub-scale courier in a CAUTIOUS, balance-of-payments-pressure regime with return on invested capital below the cost of capital should not be capitalised at the economy's nominal growth. With ROIC below WACC this growth is modelled as value-neutral to slightly negative rather than as a value driver.

challenges.challenge: The 25%-weighted EV/EBITDA cross-check is computed on the pack EBITDA of Rp18.484bn (fund record methods.ev_ebitda.metric) while the headline correction restates FY2025 EBITDA to Rp24.958bn, a 26% gap the report calls the single most important correction in the model. Fixing only the multiple basis lifts that method from Rp150 to about Rp223 and the target from Rp143 to about Rp160 (-37%, not -44%). It is also why the report can say the bull case does not reach the price: the sensitivity grid corner (revenue +4pp a year, gross margin +2pp) is Rp234, and the corrected multiple moves that corner above Rp254.
challenges.answer: The cross-check is now on the restated basis: the engine applies the 7.2x peer median to restated LTM EBITDA of Rp25.0bn, not the pack's Rp18.5bn. EV/EBITDA is Rp179 a share against the DCF's Rp82, a 118% divergence, and the blend is 70/30 after the P/E was dropped. The bull case is now Rp281, above the Rp254 price, so the bull-cannot-reach claim is withdrawn [S4][S3][S0].

challenges.challenge: All four bridge items carry probability 1.0 and together are worth Rp138.3bn, 130% of the Rp106.3bn equity value and 65% of the market cap. Two are not certain: the Rp45.3bn Mitra Samudra mark is Level 3, from a valuation report dated 11 February 2026 and unchanged at both 30 Sep 2026 and 31 Dec 2025, on a 13.67% stake in an unlisted company carried at 4.3x the Rp10.6bn cost; and the Rp20.7bn Depok land advance is, per s5 and s7, still in permitting and could be impaired. The report says the bridge total is close to the other-assets-less-other-liabilities plug, but other assets are only Rp24.9bn (S3), so that cannot validate Rp138.3bn because restricted cash and the investment are separate lines.
challenges.answer: All four bridge items now carry explicit probabilities: restricted cash and the tax refund at full weight, the Level-3 Mitra Samudra stake at 0.75 and the permitting-stage Depok land at 0.5. The other-assets cross-check is withdrawn as wrong, because other assets are a different population and the plug carries lease and tax balances [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF justification for a -44% expected return says debt of Rp166.0bn and unrestricted cash of Rp20.2bn give an EV of about Rp354bn, roughly 12.9x restated EBITDA. That EV contradicts the view embedded in the same model: subtracting the Rp138.3bn of non-operating assets leaves an operating EV of Rp219bn, or 8.0x FY2026E EBITDA, a 12% premium to the 7.15x peer median rather than a 60-80% one. The same paragraph calls Rp27.5bn restated LTM EBITDA when it is the FY2026E forecast, and the packet simultaneously quotes 11.8x FY2026E.
challenges.answer: The extreme-call justification is rebuilt on the operating EV consistent with the bridge, with LTM EBITDA stated at Rp25.0bn, not the FY2026E forecast. Section 4 now says the price pays a premium to the 7.2x peer median after bridge credit, that the sensitivity grid reaches the price only at best-margin, worst-growth, and that this is a margin-and-shrink path rather than growth [S3][S0].

challenges.challenge: The bear case depends on operating cash flow being negative in every year of the record and on the business converting almost nothing into cash. The latest filing contradicts both: 9M2026 net cash from operating activities was +Rp8.12bn against -Rp20.56bn in 9M2025, with cash receipts from customers of Rp352.6bn on revenue of Rp346.5bn and receivables down Rp11.3bn to Rp174.5bn (S3 p.8 and p.36). One signpost the report names, a year of positive operating cash flow, is largely met, and the earnings-quality conclusion of deteriorating cash conversion is stale.
challenges.answer: Section 3 is rewritten on the 9M2026 filing: operating cash flow of +Rp8.12bn against a large outflow a year earlier, cash receipts of Rp352.55bn on revenue of Rp346.46bn, and receivables down to Rp174.54bn. FY2026E FCFF is Rp9.0bn; the earnings-quality "cash conversion deteriorating" conclusion is withdrawn, while the rating stays because the cash services debt, not equity [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The 44.5% GDEX block (Gdex Sea 18.00%, Gd Express Carrier 16.50%, Gd Valueguard 10.00%) alongside a 8.94% float of 74.5m shares is not only a governance discount: it is an option on a strategic take-out or a group capital injection, and the report assigns it neither value nor probability. Equity of Rp214.5bn against a Rp211.7bn market cap, with a near-fully-depreciated asset base (accumulated depreciation Rp90.8bn on gross fixed assets of about Rp96bn) and no goodwill, also gives an asset floor that is never tested.
challenges.answer: The GDEX block is now a sized bull case: a group take-out or injection at the peer EV/EBITDA plus operating improvement reaches Rp281, above the Rp254 price, and the 25% bull weight is stated as the price of that option. The asset backing is tested separately: book equity Rp212.1bn, no goodwill, accumulated depreciation Rp90.8bn on gross PP&E of Rp96.0bn [S6][S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: The report calls refinancing high impact and the receivables book high risk, then builds a 25% bear scenario that shocks only revenue growth (-4pp) and gross margin (-2pp). Neither risk is in any scenario. The exposure is testable: Rp98.3bn of long-term bank loans due within twelve months plus Rp93.0bn short-term (notes 12 and 21, S3), secured on Rp64.9bn of deposits the company itself holds, with interest of Rp12.95bn against EBITDA of Rp27.5bn and no committed long-dated facility disclosed; and Rp177.9bn of gross receivables provisioned at 1.9% with Rp8.85bn over 90 days.
challenges.answer: The two highest-ranked risks are now inside the scenario arithmetic: the bear case adds ten points of revenue to working capital for the receivables stress and one point to WACC for a revolving line not being rolled, alongside the mirrored revenue and margin shocks [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 6 states that no rights issue, private placement, buyback or share issuance appears in the record, and the share_change assumption repeats it. The FY2025 annual report (p.127) records that the Board explained the non-implementation of the Capital Increase with Pre-emptive Rights (PM-HMETD I) approved by the EGMS of 21 August 2023, and p.45 lists the GMS approval. That is exactly the structure flag the earnings-quality card requires (a rights issue in preparation, a per-share value leak), and it is a live financing option for a company with Rp98.3bn of debt maturing inside a year.
challenges.answer: Section 6 and the share_change basis are corrected: the EGMS of 21 August 2023 approved PM-HMETD I, the FY2025 annual report records non-implementation and the AGMS accepted the explanation, and no size, price or proceeds is disclosed. No issuance is modelled because no mandate is in force, but the dilution and financing option is flagged as a signpost [S6].

challenges.challenge: Two costs of debt are used. The model interest expense is 8.0% of opening debt, sourced from FY2025 Rp12.61bn and 9M2026 Rp9.57bn annualised, while the WACC uses kd of 9.45% (fund record coc.kd_pre_tax) and section 4 describes a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt. Using the sourced 8.0% cuts WACC from 11.95% to about 11.45%, worth roughly 6% of DCF value. Separately, the 15.5% cost of equity is 2.5pp above the compounder card band of 11-13% for IDR, and the departure is argued only rhetorically, with no sourced size or liquidity premium.
challenges.answer: One cost of debt is now stated in the P&L: the contracted 8.2% disclosed on the Permata facilities. The WACC's 9.4% is the deck's marginal corporate rate for facilities that must be refinanced inside a year, and the engine has no kd override; section 4 quantifies the downward bias. The cost of equity is pinned to the top of the 11-13% band (13.0%) via a disclosed 2.5pp adjustment, because no sourced size premium exists, and the bear adds a point [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The FY+1 margin drifts up without a source. FY2026E EBITDA margin is 5.85% against FY2025A 4.77% (calibration gap 1.08pp) and there is no qc_justification for it. Revenue of Rp470.8bn implies Q4 2026 revenue of Rp124.4bn, up 2.9% yoy after nine months at -13.9%, and Q4 EBIT of Rp6.7bn, a 5.4% margin against 3.6% in 9M2026 and 2.4% in Q4 2025; gross margin of 19.5% is above both FY2025 (18.4%) and 9M2026 (19.0%). On the engine sensitivity, 0.5pp of gross margin is worth roughly Rp8-10 of value.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is now built at the 9M2026 actual ratios: revenue of Rp450.4bn on the nine-month decline, gross margin 19.0%, SG&A 15.4%, EBIT margin 3.6%. The calibration justification is recorded in qc_justifications, attributing the small EBITDA-margin gap to falling D&A [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The P/E method carries 15% of the blend on a basis the report itself disowns: a metric of Rp4.449bn LTM earnings, described in section 4 as capitalising trough FY2025 earnings and read as not a value estimate. Keeping a knowingly meaningless input at 15% weight instead of renormalising depresses the target; on FY2027E earnings of Rp6.18bn at the same 7.82x the method would be about Rp58, not Rp42, and the DCF plus EV/EBITDA blend would be about Rp10 higher before any other correction.
challenges.answer: The P/E cross-check is dropped rather than kept at weight, because the engine applies a peer trailing multiple to trough FY2025 LTM net profit of Rp0.74bn. The remaining weights renormalise to 70/30 DCF/EV-EBITDA, justified in qc_justifications, and the forward P/E is shown as a monitoring multiple only [S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the discount rate is built from the house macro deck, but fund record drivers_used is empty: no deck variable (BI rate 5.75%, CPI 3.28%, real GDP 5.29%, USD/IDR) is read by any line. The CAUTIOUS / balance-of-payments-pressure regime is never referenced although it bears directly on a levered domestic consumer-discretionary courier, and the 4.0% terminal growth is called below long-run nominal GDP without noting that the deck implies about 8.6%.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now names the deck inputs the model reads (rupiah risk-free, default spread, ERP, country risk premium, tax) and ties terminal growth to the deck's real GDP of 5.3% plus CPI of 3.3%, with the CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments regime stated. The engine has no separate drivers_used list for these lines; they are read directly in the COC build [S3].

challenges.challenge: Liquidity is argued both ways. The summary says the shares almost never trade and that the price can move on very little flow, yet the target applies a 0.0% liquidity discount because three-month turnover clears the fund floor. Both cannot hold: ADTV of Rp2.47bn a day equals 9.7m shares, or 13% of the 74.5m-share public float, every day. The one discretionary haircut in the target is set at zero on a figure inconsistent with the float the report relies on.
challenges.answer: The "almost never trade" claim is withdrawn and liquidity is now stated one way: turnover clears the house floor, so the explicit discount is 0% by rule, but an 8.9% float on Rp211.7bn of market cap means repeated float turnover, a position-size cap and gap risk. The two statements are reconciled rather than asserted together [S0][S6].

challenges.challenge: The pack working-capital series behind the most value-destructive assumption does not reconcile to the cash-flow statement. FY2024A FCFF is -Rp56.6bn in the model against filed OCF of -Rp27.8bn less capex of Rp4.7bn plus after-tax interest of about Rp5.5bn, a gap near Rp30bn, and the pack FY2024 NWC change of Rp74.1bn (from Rp115.96bn to Rp190.07bn) cannot be squared with it. FY2025 reconciles closely, so the defect may sit in the FY2023 base, but the same definition produces the 40% ratio and the Rp21.8bn FY2026E release.
challenges.answer: Operating NWC is restated from the filings, removing current restricted cash that the pack included and that the bridge already credits. FY2024 FCFF becomes -Rp18.3bn, reconciling to filed OCF of -Rp27.8bn less capex of Rp4.1bn plus after-tax interest; the 40% marginal ratio is set on the 2026Q3 balance sheet. FY2022-FY2023 cannot be re-derived from the archived filings, which carry only the 2024 comparative, and do not drive the forecast [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The Rp7.4bn estimated income-tax refund is carried in the bridge at full weight on the claim that most of it was received in January 2026, but fact F21 shows the FY2025 estimated claim of Rp7.395bn still outstanding at 30 Sep 2026 (prior Rp15.85bn); what was collected during 2026 is the FY2024 claim. The bridge weight therefore rests on a premise the filing contradicts.

The judge raised the same point as a NOTE.
